summary:
Çankırı province stands under the national framework of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026, finds that hostility toward LGBT people became explicit state policy during the year, driven by "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions from senior officials.

Kaos GL documented 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, most of them detentions. It also recorded 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51, and six right-to-life violations, three of which were classified as hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected.

Turkey's state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the monitoring data rely on media coverage rather than government records. The report is national in scope and records no province-specific enforcement or incidents in Çankırı.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison. The same draft would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years.

Under civil-code article 40, the draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and impose a permanent-infertility mandate. Providers could face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch has called for the draft's withdrawal.
tangentialFactors:
The draft judicial package remains unpassed as reported, but the pattern elsewhere in Turkey is that authorities act on prohibitions before they are legislated. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks, an practice legal experts argue violates Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Çankırı is an inland Anatolian province rather than a major tourist destination, but the national document-carrying rule applies throughout the country: foreign nationals must produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Any checkpoint stop is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.
localsOnly:
Trans prisoners in Turkey are placed according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; the case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, according to the Prison Insider country profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data. The profile documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no policy or staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints processes that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory records no Çankırı-specific enforcement actions, incidents, hate crimes, or police practices. The province-level entry rests entirely on the national framework; whether local police in Çankırı conduct GBT-style stops or document checks comparable to the Istanbul reporting is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been introduced, amended, or voted on since the 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch report is unresolved in this inventory. The draft's current legislative status should be verified against newer reporting before publication.

The Kaos GL figures derive from media coverage rather than official statistics, as the Turkish state keeps no hate-crime records. Regional distribution of the 313 liberty violations, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, and six right-to-life violations is not broken down in the inventory, so no share can be attributed to Çankırı.
